title: How Tabloids Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore the history and mechanics of tabloids. They open with the Weekly World News and its fabricated "bat boy" stories, then trace the word "tabloid" from a pharmaceutical pill name to a newspaper format. The history covers the nineteenth-century penny press, William Randolph Hearst and yellow journalism, Generoso Pope Jr. and the National Enquirer's move into supermarkets, Rupert Murdoch's News of the World, and American Media Inc.'s ownership of the major U.S. tabloids. They describe tabloid techniques: unverified quotes attributed to supposed experts, blowing up minor stories, informants, celebrity tipsters, and paparazzi (named after a Fellini character). They then cover libel law and the malice standard, celebrity lawsuits (Carol Burnett v. the National Enquirer, Elizabeth Taylor, Katie Holmes), the "scorpion defense," the News of the World phone-hacking scandal, tabloid scoops (O.J. Simpson shoes, Gary Hart, Rush Limbaugh), and declining circulation. The episode ends with listener mail from a Fulbright scholar in Argentina.

segments.title: Opening banter and Weekly World News bat boy
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the mood of the day, then discuss the Weekly World News and its fabricated bat boy stories, including its tagline calling itself the world's only reliable newspaper, and its 2008 move online.

segments.title: Origin of the word tabloid
segments.summary: The hosts discuss an etymology of 'tabloid' from Burroughs Wellcome's compressed pill called a tabloid, which came to mean a small dose, and then the term's use for a smaller newspaper format compared with broadsheets.

segments.title: Early newspapers and the penny press
segments.summary: Early nineteenth-century newspapers were expensive, dry and fact-based. The penny press made papers cheaper and shifted toward human interest stories with shorter sentences and more emotion.

segments.title: Yellow journalism, Hearst, and Generoso Pope Jr.
segments.summary: William Randolph Hearst's New York Journal popularized sensational celebrity and crime stories. After the Depression, Generoso Pope Jr. bought a Hearst paper, converted it to tabloid size, and began publishing gory crime photos, which helped launch the National Enquirer.

segments.title: Murdoch, supermarkets, and the National Enquirer's transformation
segments.summary: Rupert Murdoch's News of the World showed that sex scandals could sell millions of copies. Pope renamed and reshaped the National Enquirer, toning down the gore and adding celebrity and astrology content so it could be sold in supermarket checkout lines. The hosts cite a Vanity Fair article describing the staff's reaction.

segments.title: Tabloids and glossy magazines like People
segments.summary: The hosts note that People and US Weekly borrowed tabloid techniques, and that the Star moved to a glossy format in the late nineties, combining glossy and tabloid styles.

segments.title: Tabloid ownership and what defines a tabloid
segments.summary: American Media, Inc. owns the major U.S. tabloids, including the National Enquirer, Star, Globe, National Examiner and Weekly World News, and shut down the Weekly World News after large losses. The hosts then describe how tabloid stories rely on attributed quotes, not truth, and on unqualified experts.

segments.title: Informants, celebrity tipsters, and paparazzi
segments.summary: Tabloids get stories from informants such as security staff and salon workers, and from gossip columnists like Janet Charlton. A story about a British cop tipping off reporters about a star's daughter is recounted, with a tragic outcome. Celebrities either fight the tabloids, stay out of them, or 'play ball' by leaking information. Paparazzi are discussed as named after Fellini's character and as intensified by Pope.

segments.title: Libel law, celebrity lawsuits, and the scorpion defense
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why celebrities rarely sue, the 1981 Carol Burnett lawsuit against the National Enquirer and its reduction and settlement, and the tabloid tactic of overwhelming litigants (Elizabeth Taylor, Aretha Franklin, Katie Holmes). Libel requires malice, and tabloid articles are vetted by lawyers. The 'scorpion defense' is explained, with a scorpion tangent.

segments.title: Phone hacking, tabloid scoops, and declining sales
segments.summary: The News of the World phone hacking scandal is summarized, including the Milly Dowler case and the Rupert Murdoch parliamentary fallout. The hosts list tabloid scoops (O.J. Simpson's shoes, Gary Hart, Rush Limbaugh) and note circulation declines as mainstream media adopted tabloid tactics.

segments.title: Listener mail from Argentina
segments.summary: A listener on a Fulbright scholarship in Argentina writes that the podcast helps English learners and introduces US culture. The hosts discuss a documentary about the musician Rodriguez.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts plug the website search for tabloids and the show's social media and email, then sign off.
